data.title: QuickLtd (TSE:4318) Posted Healthy Earnings But There Are Some Other Factors To Be Aware Of

Examining Cashflow Against QuickLtd's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

Over the twelve months to September 2026, QuickLtd recorded an accrual ratio of 0.22. We can therefore deduce that its free cash flow fell well short of covering its statutory profit. To wit, it produced free cash flow of JP¥2.8b during the period, falling well short of its reported profit of JP¥4.21b. QuickLtd's free cash flow actually declined over the last year, but it may bounce back next year, since free cash flow is often more volatile than accounting profits. However, that's not all there is to consider. We can see that unusual items have impacted its statutory profit, and therefore the accrual ratio.

Given the accrual ratio, it's not overly surprising that QuickLtd's profit was boosted by unusual items worth JP¥1.1b in the last twelve months. While we like to see profit increases, we tend to be a little more cautious when unusual items have made a big contribution. When we analysed the vast majority of listed companies worldwide, we found that significant unusual items are often not repeated. And, after all, that's exactly what the accounting terminology implies. Assuming those unusual items don't show up again in the current year, we'd thus expect profit to be weaker next year (in the absence of business growth, that is).

Our Take On QuickLtd's Profit Performance

Examining Cashflow Against Sun-Wa Technos' Earnings

One key financial ratio used to measure how well a company converts its profit to free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

For the year to September 2026, Sun-Wa Technos had an accrual ratio of 0.24. We can therefore deduce that its free cash flow fell well short of covering its statutory profit. In the last twelve months it actually had negative free cash flow, with an outflow of JP¥4.9b despite its profit of JP¥4.28b, mentioned above. We saw that FCF was JP¥7.1b a year ago though, so Sun-Wa Technos has at least been able to generate positive FCF in the past. The good news for shareholders is that Sun-Wa Technos' accrual ratio was much better last year, so this year's poor reading might simply be a case of a short term mismatch between profit and FCF. Shareholders should look for improved cashflow relative to profit in the current year, if that is indeed the case.

data.title: Did Job Cuts Just Shift Wells Fargo's (WFC) Investment Narrative?
data.description:
• Wells Fargo is cutting a further 173 roles in Iowa and Virginia as part of an ongoing push to streamline operations and concentrate resources in technology and other growth areas, while continuing to simplify its wider business footprint.
  • The bank is pairing these workforce reductions with business exits and process simplification. This signals a sharper focus on long term cost efficiency and profit durability, even as it reports strong revenue and earnings.
  • Now the focus turns to how Wells Fargo's investment narrative absorbs these latest workforce cuts and what that means for the efficiency story.

Scan how Wells Fargo’s efficiency push compares with peers that already screen well on balance sheet strength and fundamentals using this curated list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals (24 results)

Wells Fargo Investment Narrative Recap

To own Wells Fargo, you need to be comfortable with a bank leaning into a larger balance sheet, expanding fee driven businesses and tightening its cost base through workforce cuts and process simplification. The recent fixed income offerings sit alongside that story, adding term funding while management keeps pushing efficiency as a key near term execution focus.

In the short term, the main swing factor remains how net interest margin and credit costs evolve as Markets financing, credit cards and investment banking build out. The biggest operational risk still sits in weaker than expected returns from newer card vintages and lower spread Markets assets, and these bond deals do not materially change that.

The most relevant fresh data point for this story is the board’s decision to affirm a US$0.50 quarterly common dividend, payable on December 1, 2026. For an investor, that matters because it signals Wells Fargo is comfortable maintaining cash returns while it issues new fixed rate senior notes and reshapes its cost base.

Those new callable senior unsecured notes, with coupons between 5.55% and 6.45% across 2030 to 2046 maturities, add another layer to the funding mix that supports loan growth, Markets activity and corporate and investment banking ambitions. The key question for you is whether that capital can be deployed in a way that offsets net interest margin pressure and card profitability risks.

What The Current Forecasts Assume For Wells Fargo

Analysts are effectively asking investors to underwrite a bigger Wells Fargo that earns more on a slightly slimmer margin profile. The current set of projections leans on mid single digit loan and fee growth, cost cuts from headcount reductions and technology, and a capital plan that keeps buybacks and dividends in the mix.

On these projections, revenue is expected to compound at 7.7% a year over the next three years, while profit margins soften from 26.4% today to 23.1% by 2029. Together, those figures outline a business that grows the overall profit pool through volume and mix, even as each dollar of sales converts into a bit less bottom line than it does now.

Earnings are forecast to reach US$24.0b by 2029, compared with US$22.0b today. This is an uplift of US$2.0b in absolute profit on the consensus view, with some analysts pencilling in as much as US$27.4b if fee businesses and efficiency gains are closer to the upper end of expectations.

These assumptions sit alongside a share count that analysts expect to decline by about 4.38% a year over the next three years. If that occurs, per share figures such as earnings and dividends would be supported by fewer shares outstanding even if the total earnings pool only edges higher.

On valuation, the same consensus assumes Wells Fargo trades on a P/E multiple of 13.7x by 2029, compared with 11.0x today and 11.4x for the broader US banks group. This reflects a market view that could be willing to pay more per dollar of profit for a cleaner, more fee weighted and more efficient institution than the one investors see today.

Wells Fargo's current analyst narrative points to US$103.9b in revenue and US$24.0b in earnings by 2029. This is based on 7.7% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about US$2.0b from US$22.0b today.

Exploring Other Perspectives

Fair value estimates for Wells Fargo from four members of the Simply Wall St Community stretch from about US$97 to roughly US$142 a share, so you are looking at a wide gap between the most cautious and the most optimistic views. Layer in the funding shift from recent fixed income offerings, plus the ongoing credit card and net interest margin risks, and it becomes clear that opinions can diverge sharply.
